## Question 1 (Reporting)

a) For each of the four main sections of an empirical paper (introduction, methods, results, discussion), state in one or two sentences what that section is supposed to accomplish for the reader.

b) Pick one specific piece of information that authors frequently put in the wrong section (for example, an interpretation that belongs in the discussion but appears in the results). Explain where it belongs and why placing it correctly matters to the reader.

## Question 2 (Reviewing the Introduction and Methods)

Find a published research paper in your own area that used multiple regression, and evaluate it from the perspective of a methodological reviewer rather than as an ordinary reader. (Pick a paper you can access in full, including its tables.) Give the full citation, then answer the following.

a) Report what you found in the **introduction**. Are the hypotheses stated *before* the results? Is the study framed as confirmatory or exploratory, and does anything (such as a preregistration) make that framing credible? (See Lecture 14b.)

b) Report what you found in the **methods**. Is the sample size justified, for example by a power analysis (Lecture 14a)? Are the variables described clearly enough that you can tell what was measured? How was the regression specified: which predictors and covariates were included, and how were outliers handled (Lecture 10b)?

## Question 3 (Reviewing the Results and Discussion)

Using the same paper you evaluated in Question 2, write a summary of what you found regarding the **results and discussion** sections.

a) Report what you found in the **results**, using the eight results-section questions from lecture as your checklist. Then say whether the claims in the **discussion** are supported by the analyses actually conducted.

b) Include a few sentences about what you learned from reviewing a paper this way, and one thing you will do differently in your own writing as a result.
